# Background {#sec-background}

The consequences of automation differ across places because every place does not depend on the same kinds of work. @Autor2003 provided the framework for explaining why, arguing that rather than automating occupations wholesale, technology replaces the specific tasks within them that can be reduced to explicit rules. Routine tasks are the easiest to specify in that form, while work depending on judgment, adaptation, or direct interaction resists it. This distinction produces the four task groups used throughout this study, namely routine cognitive, routine manual, non-routine cognitive, and non-routine manual work.

Once work is understood in terms of tasks, differences between local economies become quantifiable. @AutorDorn2013 demonstrated that these differences persist across local labor markets, where they are linked to long-term employment polarization. Regions with more routine work experienced a decline in middle-wage employment, while employment grew at both the lower and higher ends of the wage distribution. This polarization is traced using the occupation taxonomy employed in this study to categorize occupations into task groups. @AcemogluAutor2011 explained the economic significance of these differences by modeling tasks as the production units over which workers with varying skills compete. Technological advancements alter the advantages held by different workers, making the impact of technology contingent on the types of work prevalent in a local economy.

Task groups are just one aspect of a county’s economic conditions, which are also characterized by three conventional indicators: poverty, unemployment, and median household income. Poverty identifies households with limited resources, unemployment reflects access to work, and median household income describes the income received by households. However, none of these indicators alone accurately represent the conditions faced by residents.

Median household income is preferred because it more accurately reflects the typical income of households compared to the mean, which is more susceptible to the influence of high incomes in a positively skewed distribution [@Chiripanhura2011]. Since median income reflects the actual income households receive, rather than their purchasing power, and considering the varying local prices, the same nominal income can support different living standards in different regions. Purchasing power addresses this by adjusting income with Regional Price Parities, which allows for a more nuanced comparison of counties rather than a uniform adjustment.

@fig-county-context mapped the three conventional measures across counties, along with the Regional Price Parities used to adjust income. The poverty and unemployment maps revealed varying concentrations of economic distress. The median household income map depicted where household resources were highest and lowest before considering local prices. The Regional Price Parity map highlighted areas with relatively high or low prices. These patterns didn’t align across counties. Together, they demonstrated the need for purchasing power to account for what income could buy locally. The geographic scale also played a role. Much of the previous literature examined broader labor market areas that grouped several counties together, potentially combining counties with different local prices. A county-level design preserved this variation.

```{python}
#| label: context-setup
#| include: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine = create_engine(
    os.environ["AUTORACK_URL"],
    pool_pre_ping=True,
    pool_recycle=300
)
```


```{python}
#| label: county-context-data
#| include: false
context_year = 2023
context_df = pd.read_sql("""
    select cb.county_fips, cb.poverty_rate, cb.unemployment_rate,
           cb.median_household_income, ca.affordability_salary as purchasing_power
    from county_baseline cb
    join county_affordability ca
      on ca.county_fips = cb.county_fips and ca.year = cb.year
    where cb.year = %(yr)s
""", engine, params={"yr": context_year})
context_df["fips"] = context_df["county_fips"].astype(str).str.zfill(5)
# RPP recovered from the already computed purchasing power measure (@eq-afford, inverted):
# purchasing power = income / (RPP / 100), so RPP = income / purchasing power * 100.
context_df["rpp"] = context_df["median_household_income"] / context_df["purchasing_power"] * 100

gdf_context = gpd.read_file(
    "https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2021/shp/cb_2021_us_county_500k.zip"
)
gdf_context = gdf_context.rename(columns={"GEOID": "fips"})
merged_context = gdf_context.merge(
    context_df[["fips", "poverty_rate", "unemployment_rate",
                "median_household_income", "rpp"]],
    on="fips", how="left"
)
merged_context = merged_context[
    ~merged_context["STATEFP"].isin(["02", "15", "60", "66", "69", "72", "78"])
].copy()

pov_ctx_vmin = float(context_df["poverty_rate"].quantile(0.02))
pov_ctx_vmax = float(context_df["poverty_rate"].quantile(0.98))
unemp_ctx_vmin = float(context_df["unemployment_rate"].quantile(0.02))
unemp_ctx_vmax = float(context_df["unemployment_rate"].quantile(0.98))
inc_ctx_vmin = float(context_df["median_household_income"].quantile(0.02))
inc_ctx_vmax = float(context_df["median_household_income"].quantile(0.98))
rpp_ctx_vmin = float(context_df["rpp"].quantile(0.02))
rpp_ctx_vmax = float(context_df["rpp"].quantile(0.98))

os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)
merged_context[["fips", "poverty_rate", "unemployment_rate",
                "median_household_income", "rpp", "geometry"]].to_file(
    "output/county_context.geojson", driver="GeoJSON"
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-county-context
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "**Four Views of County Economic Conditions.** A) Poverty rate and B) unemployment rate, both in percent, describe economic distress. C) Median household income, in dollars, describes household resources before local prices are taken into account. D) Regional Price Parity, an index with the national average set to 100, shows how local prices vary. All panels cover the continental United States in 2023, are clipped at the 2nd and 98th percentiles, and show counties without a value in gray."
%%R -i pov_ctx_vmin -i pov_ctx_vmax -i unemp_ctx_vmin -i unemp_ctx_vmax -i inc_ctx_vmin -i inc_ctx_vmax -i rpp_ctx_vmin -i rpp_ctx_vmax -w 10 -h 9 -u in -r 150 -b transparent
suppressMessages(library(sf))

context_sf <- st_read("output/county_context.geojson", quiet=TRUE)

context_panel_theme <- theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position="bottom", legend.key.width=unit(1.1, "cm"),
        plot.title=element_text(face="bold", size=11, hjust=0.5),
        plot.background=element_rect(fill=NA, color=NA))

bottom_guide <- guide_colorbar(direction="horizontal", title.position="bottom", title.hjust=0.5)

p_pov <- ggplot(context_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=poverty_rate), color="white", linewidth=0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="#FCFCFB", high=ORANGE, limits=c(pov_ctx_vmin, pov_ctx_vmax),
                      oob=scales::squish, na.value="#EEEEEE", name="Poverty Rate (%)",
                      guide=bottom_guide) +
  coord_sf(crs=st_crs(5070), datum=NA) +
  context_panel_theme +
  labs(title="Poverty Rate")

p_unemp <- ggplot(context_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=unemployment_rate), color="white", linewidth=0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="#FCFCFB", high=PINK, limits=c(unemp_ctx_vmin, unemp_ctx_vmax),
                      oob=scales::squish, na.value="#EEEEEE", name="Unemployment Rate (%)",
                      guide=bottom_guide) +
  coord_sf(crs=st_crs(5070), datum=NA) +
  context_panel_theme +
  labs(title="Unemployment Rate")

p_inc <- ggplot(context_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=median_household_income), color="white", linewidth=0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="#FCFCFB", high=GREEN, limits=c(inc_ctx_vmin, inc_ctx_vmax),
                      oob=scales::squish, na.value="#EEEEEE",
                      labels=function(v) sprintf("$%.0fk", v/1000),
                      name="Median Household Income",
                      guide=bottom_guide) +
  coord_sf(crs=st_crs(5070), datum=NA) +
  context_panel_theme +
  labs(title="Median Household Income")

p_rpp <- ggplot(context_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=rpp), color="white", linewidth=0.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="#FCFCFB", high=BLUE, limits=c(rpp_ctx_vmin, rpp_ctx_vmax),
                      oob=scales::squish, na.value="#EEEEEE",
                      name="Regional Price Parity",
                      guide=bottom_guide) +
  coord_sf(crs=st_crs(5070), datum=NA) +
  context_panel_theme +
  labs(title="Regional Price Parity")

(p_pov | p_unemp) / (p_inc | p_rpp) +
  plot_annotation(title="Four Views of County Economic Conditions",
                  tag_levels="A", tag_suffix=")",
                  theme=theme(plot.title=element_text(face="bold", size=13, hjust=0.5),
                              plot.tag=element_text(face="bold", size=11, color="#0B0B0B")))
```

One final consideration revolved around the functional form of the relationship between task groups and purchasing power. A fixed dollar specification assumed that a consistent shift in task groups would result in a uniform dollar difference in purchasing power across counties. In contrast, a proportional specification allowed the dollar difference to fluctuate based on the level of purchasing power. The analysis aimed to determine which form more accurately represented the observed relationship.

These considerations collectively defined the gap that this study sought to address. Previous research highlighted the significance of task groups in local labor markets, while conventional economic measures focused on other aspects of county conditions. Neither of these studies established a connection between task groups and the purchasing power of households within their respective counties. Additionally, existing research explored broader labor market areas that could average over price variations between counties. Finally, prior work lacked a definitive conclusion on whether the relationship between task groups and purchasing power was better represented in fixed dollar amounts or proportionally.
